source: CARDI/MAFF Cashew Variety Guides (compiled from 3 sourced technical documents)
text:
Farmer-preferred cashew varieties in Cambodia today, per two separate source documents (which partially disagree -- included here for comparison rather than picking one): one source lists M-23, M-7, and S-40 as the newest varieties farmers prefer most; another source lists M-23, M-1, and H-09. Both sources agree M-23 is a top pick. All these newer varieties are preferred because they resist disease and pests better than older local varieties, grow and branch faster, and produce larger seeds.

What makes a cashew variety high-yielding -- criteria to look for: 10-30 flower clusters per square meter of canopy (more is better); 200-300 male flowers and 40-80 bisexual (fruit-producing) flowers per cluster (more bisexual flowers means higher yield potential); average seed weight of 7-9 grams (roughly 120-150 seeds per kilogram); kernel content of at least 28%; a short flowering period of 1-3 months; and general resistance to local pests, disease, and climate conditions. A mature tree (15+ years old) should yield 15-25 kg per year; a young tree around 8 years old should already exceed 10 kg per year.

Flowering timing matters for yield protection, and varieties fall into three general timing categories: early-flowering varieties bloom September to December, during the rainy season, which risks flowers being damaged and washed away by rain; mid-flowering varieties bloom late December to late January; late-flowering ('lazy flower') varieties, often bred for resistance, bloom late January to late February, which avoids the worst rain damage but risks flower/bud damage from cold spells or high heat above 38C. Overall, varieties that flower mid-to-late season (January-March) are generally preferred, since this timing avoids both peak tea mosquito bug activity and the heaviest rains.

One region-specific note: an 'AB' cashew variety from Stung Treng province was specifically noted as resistant to local climate variation.
